questions.prompt: A login query concatenates the submitted username into SQL. Which change addresses the injection boundary?

choices.text: Allow any SQL syntax when the request uses HTTPS.
Hide database error messages but keep the concatenation.
Bind the username as a parameter.
Base64-encode the username before concatenating it.

questions.explanation: A bound parameter is treated as data. Encoding, HTTPS and quieter errors do not remove executable string concatenation.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Parameterized queries separate code from data; safely implemented stored procedures also help, but concatenated dynamic SQL remains risky.

questions.prompt: A user chooses the column used by ORDER BY. What is the appropriate boundary?

choices.text: Allow arbitrary SQL after removing all whitespace.
Map the choice to an allowlist of known columns.
Bind a column name as an ordinary data-value parameter.
Concatenate every requested identifier if login succeeded.

questions.explanation: Parameters represent data values rather than identifiers. A fixed mapping controls executable structure; login and whitespace removal do not.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Table names, column names and sort direction cannot be bound as data values; map permitted inputs to known identifiers.

questions.prompt: A server downloads any URL submitted by a user. Which risk distinguishes SSRF?

choices.text: It may reach internal resources using server network access.
It is limited to destinations the user’s browser can directly reach.
It only matters when the URL contains an invalid hostname.
It requires the response to contain executable JavaScript.

questions.explanation: SSRF abuses server-side network reachability. Browser navigation, private-key theft and JavaScript execution are separate concerns.

sources.title: Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SSRF controls validate allowed domains and IP destinations and account for alternate representations and DNS resolution.

questions.prompt: An allowlisted URL redirects to an internal service. Which behavior enables this bypass?

choices.text: A narrow list of destination protocols.
A deny rule for private network destinations.
An egress firewall enforcing the intended reachability.
Unrestricted automatic redirect following.

questions.explanation: Redirects can switch destinations after initial validation. Protocol and network restrictions help prevent rather than create this bypass.

sources.title: Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SSRF defenses include disabling redirects where possible, constraining protocols and applying network egress restrictions.

questions.prompt: A search value contains a quote character. How should a parameterized query handle it?

choices.text: Treat quoted input as trusted executable SQL by default.
Remove parameter binding because quotes change its purpose.
Pass the full value as data through the parameter API.
Switch to concatenation whenever a value contains a quote.

questions.explanation: Binding handles the value as data, including quotes. Switching to executable concatenation removes the security boundary.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Data-value parameters keep submitted data separate from SQL syntax.

questions.prompt: A grid sends a requested sort direction. Which implementation fits OWASP guidance?

choices.text: Allow any direction string when the column exists.
Map approved values to ASC or DESC.
Concatenate the entire request field into the SQL clause.
Bind the entire ORDER BY clause as a scalar data value.

questions.explanation: Sort direction is SQL structure. A narrow fixed mapping is appropriate; ordinary value binding and unchecked concatenation are not.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SQL sort direction needs a fixed mapping instead of arbitrary executable input.

questions.prompt: Which SQL value-handling statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Review stored procedures that construct dynamic SQL internally.
Trust every stored procedure regardless of its implementation.
Use escaping as the preferred universal solution for every database.
An ORM makes every raw concatenated query safe from SQL injection.
Bind untrusted values through a parameterized query API.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Stored procedures are not safe if they concatenate executable input. B is incorrect: Dynamic SQL can preserve injection risk. C is incorrect: OWASP discourages fragile escaping as the primary defense. D is incorrect: Using an ORM does not protect raw SQL that interpolates executable input. E is correct: The database distinguishes values from SQL syntax.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Parameterized queries separate code from data; safely implemented stored procedures also help, but concatenated dynamic SQL remains risky.

questions.prompt: Which controls fit dynamic SQL structure? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Treat identifier parameters as interchangeable with value parameters.
Accept arbitrary table names from an authenticated browser.
Redesign a query when arbitrary dynamic structure is unnecessary.
Map sort-column choices to predefined identifiers.
Validate sort direction against the supported fixed options.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Databases do not use value parameters as schema identifiers. B is incorrect: Authenticated input can still contain unsafe SQL structure. C is correct: Removing dynamic structure reduces the attack surface. D is correct: An allowlist limits SQL structure. E is correct: Ascending or descending choices need controlled mapping.

sources.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Table names, column names and sort direction cannot be bound as data values; map permitted inputs to known identifiers.

questions.prompt: Which destination controls reduce SSRF risk? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Resolving an approved hostname once guarantees all future resolved addresses are safe.
Treat a URL syntax check as sufficient network authorization.
Allow only the destinations required by the feature.
Validate IP addresses against prohibited internal destinations.
Trust any hostname merely because its text looks public.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: DNS resolution can change or expose bypasses, so destination policy must account for it. B is incorrect: Valid syntax does not make a destination safe. C is correct: A constrained allowlist reduces reachable targets. D is correct: Server-accessible internal targets need protection. E is incorrect: DNS and alternate representations can defeat superficial checks.

sources.title: Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SSRF controls validate allowed domains and IP destinations and account for alternate representations and DNS resolution.

questions.prompt: Which layers help protect a server URL-fetch feature? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume URL parsing alone blocks every SSRF technique.
Disable automatic redirects when they are not required.
Restrict the permitted protocols to the feature’s needs.
Use network egress controls as well as application validation.
Permit all private networks after a public URL is validated once.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Parsing is not destination or network authorization. B is correct: Redirects can bypass initial destination validation. C is correct: Unexpected schemes increase attack surface. D is correct: Network controls limit the server’s reachability. E is incorrect: A later destination can still reach sensitive services.

sources.title: Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: SSRF defenses include disabling redirects where possible, constraining protocols and applying network egress restrictions.
